content:
Acupuncture is not recommended by NICE as a treatment for osteoarthritis, and it is not usually offered on the NHS for arthritis. Some people say it eases pain for a short time, and NICE does allow a single course of acupuncture to be considered for chronic primary pain. But exercise, weight management and good pain-relief planning remain the treatments with the strongest backing.

What acupuncture is

Acupuncture involves placing very fine, sterile needles into the skin at chosen points. It comes from traditional Chinese medicine. In the UK it is also practised by some physiotherapists and doctors, who often call it "dry needling" or "Western medical acupuncture". They explain any effect in terms of nerves and pain signals, not energy flow.

A session usually lasts 20 to 40 minutes. Most people feel a brief prick, then a dull ache or tingling around the needle. A course is typically several weekly sessions.

What UK guidance says

NICE's osteoarthritis guideline (NG226) says do not offer acupuncture or dry needling for osteoarthritis. The evidence did not show a meaningful benefit over sham (pretend) acupuncture.

For low back pain and sciatica, NICE (NG59) also advises against acupuncture.

For chronic primary pain, meaning long-term pain with no clear underlying cause such as fibromyalgia, NICE (NG193) says a single course of acupuncture can be considered. It should be delivered by a trained practitioner, within a defined course and in a community setting. This guidance does not cover pain caused by arthritis damage itself, but some people with arthritis also have widespread pain that falls under it.

Why some people still feel it helps

People's experiences vary, and short-term relief is real for some. Possible reasons include:

  • the relaxing setting and one-to-one time
  • distraction and a change in how the nervous system processes pain
  • natural ups and downs in arthritis pain, so improvement may happen anyway
  • expectation, which genuinely affects how much pain we feel

None of this makes acupuncture harmful. It means it is best treated as an optional extra rather than a replacement for proven care.

Is it safe?

In trained hands acupuncture is generally low risk. Common minor effects are small bruises, soreness or feeling light-headed. Talk to your GP or rheumatology team first if you:

  • take blood thinners such as warfarin or a DOAC, or have a bleeding disorder
  • take biologics, methotrexate or steroids, which can raise your infection risk
  • have a pacemaker (some practitioners use electro-acupuncture)
  • are pregnant
  • have lymphoedema or a joint replacement near the treatment area

Practitioners should use single-use needles. Choose someone registered with a professional body, or a physiotherapist registered with the HCPC.

Cost and access in the UK

Acupuncture for arthritis is rarely available on the NHS. Some NHS physiotherapy and pain services offer it for other conditions. Privately, prices vary by area and practitioner. Ask for the full cost of a course before you start, and set yourself a review point. If you notice no real change after three or four sessions, it is reasonable to stop.

What to try first

If you are thinking about acupuncture because your pain is not well controlled, these steps are recommended by NICE and are often more effective:

  • Regular, tailored exercise. Strengthening and general activity is the core treatment for osteoarthritis. A physiotherapist can build a plan around your joints.
  • Weight management. If you are carrying extra weight, losing some reduces load on knees and hips.
  • A pain-relief review. Topical anti-inflammatory gels for knee and hand osteoarthritis are often overlooked. Your pharmacist can advise.
  • Heat, cold and pacing. These are simple ways to calm flare-ups at home.
  • TENS. Some people find it useful for short-term relief at home after a one-off cost.

If you have inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis, the most important treatment is disease-modifying medicine prescribed by your rheumatology team. Acupuncture will not control inflammation or prevent joint damage.

Questions to ask before booking

  • What training and registration do you have?
  • How many sessions do you suggest, and what will it cost in total?
  • How will we judge whether it is working?
  • Do you need to know about my medicines?

Keep a short pain diary before and during the course. It will show you honestly whether it is worth continuing.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
